v.q: Which probe decides whether a pod receives traffic from a Service?
o: None: the Service always uses every running pod
v.w: A failing readiness probe removes the pod from the Service endpoints without restarting it.

v.q: What happens when a liveness probe fails enough times?
o: The pod is removed from the Service but kept running
v.w: The pod stays; its container is killed and started again.

v.q: Which HTTP status codes count as a successful httpGet probe?
v.w: 401, 404, 500 and 503 are failures.

v.q: What does a tcpSocket probe prove?
o: Only that something accepts connections on the port
That the application can reach its database
That the HTTP health endpoint returns 200
That the container has enough memory
v.w: It says nothing about the health of the application.

v.q: With default settings, about how long until a hung container fails liveness?
o: About 30 seconds (3 failures at a 10 second period)
v.w: periodSeconds 10 and failureThreshold 3.

v.q: What is the default timeoutSeconds, and why is it often raised?
o: 1 second; a GC pause or CPU throttling can easily exceed it
10 seconds; it is the same as the period
v.w: A timeout counts as a failure.

v.q: What do liveness and readiness do while the startup probe has not succeeded yet?
o: They run but their failures are ignored
v.w: Startup protects slow starts from the liveness probe.

v.q: A JVM needs up to 120 seconds to start. Which startup probe settings fit?
v.w: The budget is failureThreshold times periodSeconds.

v.q: Why is a startup probe better than a large initialDelaySeconds on liveness?
o: A fast start continues as soon as it succeeds, while a slow start still gets its full budget
initialDelaySeconds is not allowed on liveness
A startup probe also restarts the node
v.w: A fixed delay always waits the whole time.

v.q: What happens if the startup probe never succeeds within its budget?
o: The container is killed and restarted
v.w: restartPolicy then applies.

v.q: Why must a liveness probe not check the database?
o: A database outage would fail liveness on every pod and restart them all
v.w: A restart does not fix the database and removes capacity.

v.q: Which check suits a liveness endpoint?
o: A fast local check that the process can still answer
A call to every downstream service
v.w: Liveness is about this process only.

v.q: What changes when a readiness probe fails?
o: The pod's address is marked not ready in the EndpointSlice and receives no new connections
The pod is deleted and rescheduled
v.w: The container keeps running and keeps being probed.

v.q: What else treats a not-ready pod as unavailable?
o: A Deployment rollout and a PodDisruptionBudget
v.w: Readiness gates releases and disruption budgets.

v.q: The database is down and your readiness probe checks it. What happens?
o: Every pod becomes unready, the Service has no endpoints, and all requests fail
The pods restart and recover the database
v.w: Use a circuit breaker and a fallback for dependency failures.

v.q: What should readiness mostly reflect?
o: This pod's own ability to serve, including being warmed up
The health of every other service
Whether the image is the latest
v.w: Shared dependencies make all pods fail together.

v.q: Which Spring Boot endpoints back the Kubernetes probes?
v.w: Backed by LivenessState and ReadinessState.

v.q: What is the readiness state while graceful shutdown begins?
v.w: Readiness drops first so the pod stops getting new requests.

v.q: A health endpoint behind Spring Security returns 401 to the kubelet. What is the result?
o: The probe passes because 401 means the app is up
v.w: Only 200 to 399 count as success.

v.q: Why can a separate management port help?
o: Probes keep working when the request thread pool is saturated
It makes probes encrypted by default
It removes the need for any timeout
v.w: The trade-off: the main port could be stuck while the probe still passes.

v.q: With maxUnavailable 0, when is an old pod removed during a rolling update?
o: After a new pod is available, meaning Ready
As soon as the new container starts
After the new image is pulled
Immediately, before the new pod exists
v.w: Readiness gates the release.

v.q: A new version never becomes ready. What happens?
o: The rollout stalls and the old pods keep serving until someone rolls back
Kubernetes rolls back automatically at once
All old pods are removed anyway
v.w: After progressDeadlineSeconds the Deployment shows ProgressDeadlineExceeded; it does not undo itself.

v.q: What does minReadySeconds add?
o: A pod must stay Ready for that long before it counts as available
A delay before the container starts
v.w: It stops a pod that is ready and then crashes from passing the gate.

v.q: What if a Deployment has no readiness probe at all?
o: A pod is ready when its container starts, so a broken version can take traffic
v.w: Always define readiness for services.

v.q: What is the shutdown order for a deleted pod?
o: preStop, then SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period
v.w: Endpoint removal runs at the same time but is not coordinated with it.

v.q: What is the default terminationGracePeriodSeconds?
v.w: The grace period must cover preStop plus the application's shutdown.

v.q: Why add a preStop sleep of a few seconds?
o: Endpoint removal takes time to reach every node, so the app keeps serving meanwhile
To make the pod start faster
To let the database finish its backup
v.w: Otherwise some requests hit a pod that already exited.

v.q: Which condition must hold for the grace period?
o: It is larger than preStop plus the application's shutdown timeout
v.w: For example 10 + 25 is less than 45.

v.q: Pods restart at peak traffic and it gets worse. What is a likely cause?
o: Liveness timeouts under load that restart the pods carrying the traffic
The Service has too many endpoints
v.w: Keep liveness cheap and independent of load, and raise the timeout.

v.q: Which event text points to a liveness probe as the cause?
o: Liveness probe failed ... container will be restarted
v.w: Look in kubectl describe pod.

v.q: Which command shows which pod IPs are currently ready for a Service?
o: kubectl get endpointslices for the Service
v.w: kubectl get endpoints also works on older clusters.

v.q: Exit code 137 with OOMKilled points to what?
o: The container exceeded its memory limit
v.w: Not a probe problem: raise or fix memory.
